title: Maximum Average Subarray I
summary: Find the contiguous subarray of length k with the largest average and return that average.
statement:
Among all contiguous subarrays of `nums` that have exactly `k` elements, find the one with the largest average and return that average.

Answers within `1e-5` of the exact value are accepted.

Slide a window of exactly `k` elements across the array, adding the element that enters and subtracting the one that leaves, and keep the largest sum.
hints: All windows have the same length k, so the window with the largest sum also has the largest average.
Compute the sum of the first k values, then slide: add the value entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left.
Track the best sum while sliding and divide by k once at the end. Use a double (or long) for the division.
explain: The windows of 4 elements sum to 2, 51 and 42. The best is `[12,-5,-6,50]` with sum 51, and 51 / 4 = 12.75.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
summary: Return the length of the longest substring of s in which no character repeats.
statement:
Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest substring (a contiguous run of characters) in which no character appears more than once.

Note the difference between a substring and a subsequence: in `"pwwkew"` the answer is 3 (`"wke"`), because `"pwke"` skips a character and is not a substring.
constraints: `s` consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
hints: Keep a window of characters with no repeats. What should happen when the next character is already inside the window?
Grow the window on the right. When the new character is a repeat, move the left edge forward until the window is repeat-free again.
Instead of stepping the left edge one by one, remember the last index of each character and jump left to (last index + 1). Never move left backwards; "abba" tests this.
explain: The longest stretch with no repeated letter is "abc" (also "bca" and "cab"), which has length 3. Any 4 consecutive letters repeat one of them.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
summary: All values are positive. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if none exists.
statement:
`nums` contains only positive integers. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to `target`. If no subarray reaches `target`, return `0`.

Because every value is positive, growing a window only increases its sum and shrinking it only decreases it, which is what makes the two-pointer window work.
hints: Because every value is positive, adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it. That makes a sliding window safe.
Expand the window to the right until the sum reaches target, then shrink it from the left while it still does, recording the length each time.
Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so this is O(n). Start the best length at a sentinel (like n + 1) so you can return 0 when nothing qualified.
explain: The subarray `[4,3]` sums to 7, which reaches the target with just 2 elements. No single element is 7 or more, so the answer is 2.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
summary: In a binary array you may flip at most k zeros to ones. Return the longest run of consecutive ones you can get.
statement:
`nums` contains only `0`s and `1`s. You may flip at most `k` of the zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive ones you can end up with.

Equivalently, find the longest window that contains at most `k` zeros: those zeros are the ones you flip.
hints: Rephrase it: find the longest contiguous window that contains at most k zeros.
Slide a window over the array, counting the zeros inside. When the count goes above k, move the left edge until it is back to k.
The answer is the largest window size seen. k can be larger than the number of zeros, in which case the whole array works.
explain: Flip the zeros at index 5 and index 10. Then indices 5 to 10 are all ones, a run of 6, and no choice of two flips does better. The answer is 6.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
summary: You may change at most k characters of s (uppercase letters). Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.
statement:
`s` contains only uppercase English letters. You may pick any character of `s` and change it to any other uppercase letter, at most `k` times in total.

Return the length of the longest substring that can be made to consist of a single repeated letter.
hints: In a window, which characters would you change? Everything except the most frequent letter.
A window is valid when (window length − count of its most frequent letter) ≤ k. Slide a window and keep a count of each letter.
When the window becomes invalid, move the left edge by one. You never need to recompute the maximum count downward: the answer only grows when a larger maximum appears.
explain: Replace both "A"s with "B" (or both "B"s with "A") and the whole string becomes one letter repeated, length 4.

title: Permutation in String
summary: Return true if some rearrangement of s1 appears as a contiguous substring of s2 (lowercase letters).

perf.label: s2 of 10,000 characters
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(1000, "abcde"); String a1 = BCB.str(10000, "abcde");

statement:
Return `true` if `s2` contains a contiguous substring that is a rearrangement (a permutation) of `s1`, and `false` otherwise.

Both strings contain lowercase English letters only.

Only windows of exactly the length of `s1` can match, so slide a window of that size over `s2` and compare letter counts.
constraints: `s1` and `s2` have only lowercase English letters
hints: A permutation of s1 has exactly the same letter counts as s1, and the same length.
Slide a window of length s1.length over s2 and keep the letter counts of the window. Compare them with the counts of s1.
Comparing two 26-entry arrays per step is fine (O(26·n)). For O(n), keep a running count of how many letters already match.
explain: s2 contains "ba" at index 3, and "ba" is a rearrangement of "ab", so the answer is `true`.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
summary: Return every start index in s where a rearrangement of p begins, in increasing order.

perf.label: s of 30,000 characters
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(30000, "abc"); String a1 = BCB.str(1000, "abc");

statement:
Return every index `i` such that the substring of `s` that starts at `i` and has length `p.length` is an anagram (a rearrangement) of `p`. Return the indices in increasing order.

Both strings contain lowercase English letters only. If `p` is longer than `s`, the answer is empty.
constraints: `s` and `p` have only lowercase English letters
hints: This is "Permutation in String", but you collect every match instead of stopping at the first.
Keep letter counts for p and for a window of the same length sliding over s.
When the window moves, add the entering letter and remove the leaving one, then record the start index whenever the counts are equal.
explain: The substring starting at index 0 is "cba" and the one at index 6 is "bac"; both are rearrangements of "abc". No other start works, so the answer is `[0,6]`.

title: Minimum Window Substring
summary: Return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (with multiplicity), or "" if none. The answer is unique.

perf.label: s of 100,000 characters
perf.gen: String base = BCB.str(99997, "abcdefghij"); String a0 = base.substring(0, 50000) + "xyz" + base.substring(50000); String a1 = "zyx";

statement:
Return the shortest contiguous substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, including repeats (if `t` has two `a`s, the window needs at least two). If no such substring exists, return `""`.

For every input the shortest window is unique. Letters are case-sensitive.
constraints: `s` and `t` consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters
hints: Use a sliding window: expand it until it covers t, then shrink it while it still covers t.
Keep a count of what t needs and a counter of how many required characters are still missing. A character only reduces "missing" when the window needed it.
While missing == 0, record the window if it is the shortest so far, then remove the left character; if that makes it needed again, missing goes back up and you start expanding.
explain: The window "BANC" near the end contains an A, a B and a C, and it is only 4 characters long. Every other window with all three letters is longer, so the answer is "BANC".

title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
summary: Count the contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k distinct values.
statement:
A subarray is "good" if it contains exactly `k` different values. Count the good contiguous subarrays of `nums`.

For example, `[1,2,3,1,2]` has exactly 3 different values.

A useful trick: the number with exactly k different values equals the number with at most k minus the number with at most k − 1, and "at most" is easy to count with a sliding window.
hints: "Exactly k" is awkward for a sliding window, but "at most k" is easy. Can you get one from the other?
exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1).
For atMost(k): slide a window, shrink it while it has more than k distinct values, and add (right − left + 1) for every right edge. That counts all valid subarrays ending at right.
explain: The subarrays with exactly 2 different values are `[1,2]`, `[2,1]`, `[1,2]`, `[2,3]`, `[1,2,1]`, `[2,1,2]` and `[1,2,1,2]`: 7 in total.
